scenes.section_title:
* Primary Learning Objective: Formulate the kinematic equations for 1D vertical free fall motion under constant gravitational acceleration \\(a = -g\\) (\\(-9.81\text{ m/s}^2\\) or \\(-32.2\text{ ft/s}^2\\)) using an upward-directed coordinate axis \\(+y\\).
* Essential and Supporting Perspectives: Essential: Coordinate System Perspective (establishing vertical origin \\(O\\) and upward positive direction \\(+y\\)), Time Perspective (time-evolution of vertical position \\(y(t)\\) and velocity \\(v(t)\\)). Supporting: Environmental Idealization Perspective (vacuum assumption neglecting aerodynamic resistance).
* Important Evidence Gaps: Source material assumes uniform gravitational field strength \\(g\\) independent of altitude changes and neglects atmospheric drag, air buoyancy, and Earth rotation (Coriolis forces).
scenes.generated_prompt:
Process
Learning Target: Formulate vertical free-fall motion equations under constant gravitational acceleration a = -g using an upward positive coordinate axis +y.
Scene Objects and Initial State: Vertical launch ruler track marked from 0m to 100m. Sphere sprite P positioned at initial height y0 = 49.05m with initial velocity v0 = 0.0 m/s. Attached green vertical velocity arrow v (length = 0), fixed red downward acceleration arrow g (length fixed at -9.81 m/s^2). Digital display panel showing 'Time t = 0.0s', 'Height y = 49.05m', 'Velocity v = 0.0 m/s', 'Acceleration a = -9.81 m/s^2'. Side-by-side plots: Left (y-t downward parabola), Right (v-t linear downward slope).
Time Behavior: Simulated physical time playback from t = 0.0s to t = 3.0s. As time advances, sphere P drops vertically toward ground (y = 0m). Downward velocity arrow expands linearly from 0.0 m/s to -29.43 m/s, while height drops quadratically according to y(t) = 49.05 - 4.905*t^2, reaching ground at t = 3.0s.
Custom Perspectives: Coordinate Orientation Perspective: Answers 'Why does gravity carry a negative algebraic sign in vertical kinematics?'. Visualizes the upward orientation of coordinate axis +y forcing downward gravitational acceleration toward Earth to take negative value a = -g.
Governing Rules: a = -g = -9.81 m/s^2 (SI) or -32.2 ft/s^2 (Imperial); v(t) = v0 - g*t; y(t) = y0 + v0*t - 0.5*g*t^2; v^2 = v0^2 - 2*g*(y - y0).
Learner Investigations and Controls: Learner Action 1: Adjust 'Initial Velocity v0' slider from 0.0 m/s to -10.0 m/s (downward launch). Affected State: Velocity arrow initial length and flight duration. Visible Consequence: Downward velocity arrow starts at -10.0 m/s; sphere accelerates faster toward ground, hitting y = 0m at t = 2.23s instead of 3.0s. Learner Action 2: Toggle 'Gravity Unit System' from Metric (9.81 m/s^2) to Imperial (32.2 ft/s^2). Affected State: Coordinate ruler tick labels and calculation readouts. Visible Consequence: Height scale relabels to feet; acceleration readout updates to -32.2 ft/s^2; flight timing updates based on imperial parameters.
Linked Representations: Sphere position on vertical ruler track is real-time synchronized with height height on y-t parabola and velocity arrow size on v-t plot.
Visual Outcome and Misconception Contrast: Visually establishes that free fall is constant acceleration motion with a = -g directed downward, correcting the misconception that heavier objects drop faster in a vacuum than light ones.
Acceptance Requirements: Setting v0 = 0 and y0 = 49.05m must result in ground impact at t = 3.0s with velocity v = -29.43 m/s; acceleration readout must stay fixed at -9.81 m/s^2 throughout flight.
Limitations: System assumes pristine vacuum environment; air drag and atmospheric buoyancy are excluded.

* Essential and Supporting Perspectives: Essential: Coordinate System Perspective (establishing vertical origin \\(O\\) and upward positive direction \\(+y\\)), Time Perspective (time-evolution of vertical position \\(y(t)\\) and velocity \\(v(t)\\)). first_output.core_understanding:
* Baseline Concept: Free fall is a special case of 1D rectilinear motion under constant acceleration where air resistance is neglected and the sole force acting is gravity. By establishing an upward vertical axis \\(+y\\), the acceleration is fixed at \\(a = -g\\), yielding velocity \\(v(t) = v_0 - gt\\), vertical position \\(y(t) = y_0 + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2} gt^2\\), and velocity-position relation \\(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g(y - y_0)\\).
* Time Perspective: Free-fall motion unfolds continuously along the time axis \\(t\\). At initial instant \\(t = 0\\), object sits at vertical height \\(y_0\\) with launch velocity \\(v_0\\). As time progresses, constant downward acceleration \\(-g\\) continually reduces upward velocity (or increases downward speed), causing vertical height \\(y(t)\\) to trace a quadratic downward-opening parabolic path over time.
* Custom Perspectives: Coordinate System Perspective answers: "Why is gravitational acceleration defined as negative \\(-g\\)?" Defining the positive coordinate axis pointing upward (\\(+y\\)) forces the downward gravitational pull toward Earth's center to carry a negative algebraic sign (\\(a = -g\\)).
* Synthesis: Free fall integrates constant acceleration principles with a fixed vertical spatial frame, where downward gravitational acceleration \\(-g\\) governs position quadratic growth and linear velocity reduction independent of object mass.

* Position-Time Equation: \\(y(t) = y_0 + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2\text{ [m]}\\)

first_output.real_life_example:
* المثال: إلقاء حجر في بئر عميق لحساب عمقه عن طريق قياس زمن وصول الحجر للقاع.

* Primary Learning Objective: Analyze the two-way flight trajectory of an object thrown vertically upward, calculating time to maximum height \\(t_{\text{up}} = \frac{v_0}{g}\\), maximum height \\(h_{\text{max}} = y_0 + \frac{v_0^2}{2g}\\), total time of flight, and proving parabolic time symmetry.
* Essential and Supporting Perspectives: Essential: Time Perspective (symmetric upward decrescendo vs downward crescendo duration), Motion Boundary Perspective (instantaneous rest at peak position \\(v = 0\\) while \\(a = -g\\)). Supporting: Kinetic Energy Conservation Perspective (speed magnitude equality at identical heights \\(|v_{\text{up}}| = |v_{\text{down}}|\\)).
* Important Evidence Gaps: Ignores atmospheric air drag, which in reality breaks time symmetry by making downward flight duration longer than upward flight duration.

Learning Target: Calculate peak apex height h_max = y0 + v0^2 / (2g), time to apex t_up = v0 / g, and demonstrate perfect flight time and velocity symmetry for upward vertical projectiles.
Scene Objects and Initial State: Vertical launch track with ball sprite positioned at ground level y0 = 0.0m. Control slider set to 'Upward Launch Velocity v0 = +29.43 m/s'. Stage 2 (Descent: 3.0s <= t <= 6.0s): Ball falls from 44.15m back to ground; green velocity arrow flips downward and expands from 0.0 m/s to -29.43 m/s at impact (t = 6.0s).

Governing Rules: At maximum height: v_peak = 0 m/s (while a = -g); t_up = v0 / g; h_max = y0 + v0^2 / (2*g); t_flight = 2 * t_up = 2*v0 / g; v_return = -v0.

first_output.core_understanding:
* Baseline Concept: When an object is projected vertically upward with initial speed \\(v_0 > 0\\), downward gravitational acceleration \\(-g\\) decelerates the object until it reaches maximum height \\(h_{\text{max}}\\), where instantaneous velocity vanishes (\\(v = 0\\)). The object then accelerates downward. In a vacuum, the upward trip time \\(t_{\text{up}} = \frac{v_0}{g}\\) equals the downward return time \\(t_{\text{down}}\\), and the object returns to its release level with a speed equal in magnitude to its launch speed (\\(|v_{\text{return}}| = v_0\\)).
* Time Perspective: Chronological symmetry across flight duration: From launch \\(t = 0\\) to peak \\(t_{\text{up}} = \frac{v_0}{g}\\), velocity linearly decreases from \\(+v_0 \to 0\\). At peak instant \\(t = t_{\text{up}}\\), particle velocity is zero while acceleration remains strictly \\(-g\\). From peak \\(t_{\text{up}}\\) to return \\(t_{\text{total}} = \frac{2v_0}{g}\\), velocity linearly decreases from \\(0 \to -v_0\\).
* Custom Perspectives: Motion Boundary Perspective answers: "Is acceleration zero at the peak of vertical flight when velocity is zero?" Acceleration is NEVER zero during free fall; at the apex, \\(v = 0\\) but \\(a = -g\\). If acceleration were zero at the peak, the object would remain hovering motionless indefinitely.
* Synthesis: Upward vertical free fall demonstrates perfect parabolic time and velocity symmetry around its apex, where instantaneous rest (\\(v = 0\\)) occurs under non-zero constant downward gravitational acceleration \\(a = -g\\).

scenes.section_title:
* Primary Learning Objective: Analyze relative motion and interception conditions between multiple free-falling bodies dropped or launched vertically at different times or positions.
* Essential and Supporting Perspectives: Essential: Relative Motion Perspective (zero relative acceleration between free-falling objects \\(a_{\text{rel}} = 0\\)), Spatial Interception Perspective (equating position equations \\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\)). * Important Evidence Gaps: Ignores physical collision restitution elasticity, aerodynamic drafting behind leading bodies, and spatial volume overlap during interception.

Comparison
Learning Target: Analyze multi-body vertical free fall dynamics, proving zero relative acceleration a_rel = 0, constant relative velocity v_rel = const, and solving interception coordinates yA(t) = yB(t).
Scene Objects and Initial State: Vertical elevator shaft track with two sphere sprites. Object A (blue sphere) positioned at top y0A = 100.0m with initial velocity v0A = 0.0 m/s. Object B (red sphere) positioned at bottom y0B = 0.0m with initial upward launch velocity v0B = +25.0 m/s. Control controls set to 'Object B Launch Speed v0B = 25.0 m/s', 'Launch Delay td = 0.0s'. Shared graph panel displaying intersecting y-t parabolas for Object A and Object B. Digital readout showing 'a_rel = 0.0 m/s^2', 'v_rel = 25.0 m/s', 'Interception Time t = 4.0s', 'Interception Height y = 21.52m'.
Time Behavior: Simultaneous multi-body free fall execution starting at t = 0.0s. Both spheres accelerate downward under gravity (-9.81 m/s^2). Object A drops from 100m while Object B rises from ground. At t = 4.0s, both spheres reach identical vertical coordinate y = 21.52m and collide.
Custom Perspectives: Relative Motion Reference Frame Perspective: Answers 'How does an observer falling on Object A perceive the motion of Object B?'. Visualizes the elimination of gravitational acceleration in relative coordinates, making Object B appear to move at constant linear velocity.
Governing Rules: a_rel = aA - aB = (-g) - (-g) = 0; v_rel = v0A - v0B = constant; Interception condition: yA(t_intercept) = yB(t_intercept) => 100 - 0.5*g*t^2 = 25*t - 0.5*g*t^2 => 25*t = 100 => t = 4.0s.
Learner Investigations and Controls: Learner Action 1: Adjust 'Launch Delay td' slider from 0.0s to 1.0s (Object B launched 1 second after Object A drops). Affected State: Object B launch timing and interception height. Visible Consequence: Object A drops alone for 1.0s reaching y = 95.095m before Object B launches; interception point shifts lower to y = 11.23m at t = 4.21s; shared y-t plot updates intersection point. Learner Action 2: Toggle 'Reference Frame' from 'Ground Frame' to 'Object A Relative Frame'. Affected State: Visual camera perspective and background grid. Visible Consequence: Object A appears stationary at origin; Object B moves upward in a perfectly straight line at constant velocity 25.0 m/s without parabolic curvature.
Linked Representations: Dual sphere positions on elevator track are real-time synchronized with intersecting curves on shared y-t plot and relative motion readout panel.
Visual Outcome and Misconception Contrast: Visually proves that free-falling bodies experience zero relative acceleration and constant relative velocity, correcting the misconception that gravity creates complex non-linear relative motion between falling objects.
Acceptance Requirements: Interception time calculation must satisfy yA(t) = yB(t); relative acceleration readout must display 0.0 m/s^2 throughout common flight.
Limitations: Assumes point mass objects without spatial overlap volume or collision restitution elasticity.

first_output.section_identity:
* Primary Learning Objective: Analyze relative motion and interception conditions between multiple free-falling bodies dropped or launched vertically at different times or positions.
* Essential and Supporting Perspectives: Essential: Relative Motion Perspective (zero relative acceleration between free-falling objects \\(a_{\text{rel}} = 0\\)), Spatial Interception Perspective (equating position equations \\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\)). Supporting: Multi-Body Timing Perspective (phase offsets \\(\Delta t\\) in release times).
* Important Evidence Gaps: Ignores physical collision restitution elasticity, aerodynamic drafting behind leading bodies, and spatial volume overlap during interception.
first_output.core_understanding:
* Baseline Concept: When two or more bodies move vertically under free fall simultaneously, both experience identical downward acceleration \\(a_A = a_B = -g\\). Consequently, the relative acceleration between them is zero (\\(a_{\text{rel}} = a_A - a_B = 0\\)). This means the relative velocity between any two free-falling objects remains constant throughout their common flight duration (\\(v_{\text{rel}} = v_A - v_B = \text{constant}\\)). Interception or collision occurs at the instant \\(t\\) when their vertical coordinates coincide (\\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\)).
* Time Perspective: Multi-body timeline: Body A released at \\(t = 0\\); Body B launched at delayed instant \\(t = t_d\\). Prior to \\(t_d\\), Body A moves alone. For \\(t \ge t_d\\), both bodies undergo free fall with constant relative velocity. Interception instant \\(t_{\text{intercept}}\\) is solved by equating position polynomials \\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\).
* Custom Perspectives: Relative Motion Perspective answers: "How does an observer on one falling object perceive another falling object?" Since relative acceleration is zero (\\(a_{\text{rel}} = 0\\)), an observer falling on object A sees object B moving toward or away from them at a completely constant speed, as if gravity were turned off entirely.
* Synthesis: Systems of multiple free-falling objects simplify in relative coordinates because identical gravitational acceleration eliminates relative acceleration, turning complex quadratic interception problems into linear relative velocity calculations.
first_output.visual_first_explanation:
* Perspective Visibility: A two-body vertical elevator shaft simulation showing Object A dropped from the top and Object B launched upward from the bottom, accompanied by crossing position-time curves on a shared \\(y-t\\) graph.
* Metaphor vs Literal Representation: The intersection point of two parabolic curves on a \\(y-t\\) graph literally represents the physical spatial collision point of the two objects in space and time.
* Limitations of Metaphor: Graphs depict point intersections, whereas physical objects have non-zero dimensions and will collide when their surface boundaries meet.
first_output.visual_scene_script:
* Normal Explanatory Sequence: Object A dropped from top of a tower (\\(y_{0A} = 100\text{ m}\\), \\(v_{0A} = 0\\)) at \\(t = 0\\). Object B launched upward from ground (\\(y_{0B} = 0\\), \\(v_{0B} = +25\text{ m/s}\\)) at same instant \\(t = 0\\). Position equations: \\(y_A(t) = 100 - 4.905 t^2\\) and \\(y_B(t) = 25t - 4.905 t^2\\). Setting \\(y_A = y_B \implies 100 - 4.905 t^2 = 25t - 4.905 t^2 \implies 25t = 100 \implies t = 4.0\text{ s}\\). Collision occurs at height \\(y = 100 - 4.905(16) = 21.52\text{ m}\\).
* Alternative Conditions and Observable Outcomes: Object B release is delayed by \\(t_d = 1.0\text{ s}\\). Quadratic terms no longer cancel directly; learner solves shifted position equation \\(y_B(t) = 0 + v_{0B}(t - 1) - \frac{1}{2}g(t - 1)^2\\).
* Intervention and Inspection Points: Learner switches camera view to "Relative Frame of Object A", observing Object B approaching in a perfectly straight line at constant velocity \\(v_{\text{rel}} = 25\text{ m/s}\\).
first_output.dynamic_view_blueprint:

* Interaction Specifications: Learner adjusts delay slider \\(t_d\\) or launch speed \\(v_{0B}\\) \\(\to\\) curve intersection point on \\(y-t\\) shifts \\(\to\\) collision height and impact velocity update \\(\to\\) sphere sprites execute collision animation at calculated instant.
* Controls Classification: Object B Launch Velocity \\(v_{0B}\\) (boundary condition parameter); Time Delay Slider \\(t_d\\) (phase timing control); Reference Frame Selector (Earth Frame vs Object A Relative Frame).
first_output.visual_learning_outcome:
* Main Outcome: Learner solves multi-body vertical free-fall problems by establishing position equations \\(y_A(t)\\) and \\(y_B(t)\\) or utilizing constant relative velocity \\(v_{\text{rel}}\\).
* Transferable Condition: Learner recognizes that any group of objects moving under the same uniform force field (like gravity) experiences zero relative acceleration, simplifying relative motion analysis.
first_output.concept_check:
* Activity: Predict–Observe–Explain.
* Contrast Setup: Ball A is dropped from a cliff. One second later, Ball B is dropped from the same cliff. Learner predicts whether the vertical distance between Ball A and Ball B increases, decreases, or stays the same as they fall.
* Expected Observation & Explanation: The distance between Ball A and Ball B increases continuously over time. Explanation: Relative velocity \\(v_{\text{rel}} = v_A - v_B = g \cdot t_d = 9.81\text{ m/s}\\) is constant and positive. Since Ball A is moving faster than Ball B at every instant, the spatial gap \\(\Delta y = v_{\text{rel}} \cdot t\\) expands linearly with time.
first_output.conceptual_summary: * Synthesis: Multi-body free fall features zero relative acceleration (\\(a_{\text{rel}} = 0\\)) and constant relative velocity (\\(v_{\text{rel}} = \text{const}\\)). Interception positions and times are determined by setting \\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\).
first_output.colloquial_egyptian_explanation: * الشرح: لما يكون عندنا جسمين بيتحركوا رأسيًا في السقوط الحر في نفس الوقت، الاتنين تحت تأثير نفس عجلة الجاذبية (\\(a_A = a_B = -g\\)). ده معناه إن العجلة النسبية بينهم بتساوي صفر (\\(a_{\text{rel}} = a_A - a_B = 0\\))! ونتيجة لكده، السرعة النسبية بين أي جسمين في السقوط الحر بتبقى ثابته تماماً طول الرحلة (\\(v_{\text{rel}} = \text{const}\\)). ولما نحب نحسب لحظة التقاطع أو التصادم بين الجسمين في الهواء، بنساوي معادلة موضع الجسم الأول بمعادلة موضع الجسم الثاني (\\(y_A(t) = y_B(t)\\)) ونحسب زمن التقاطع.
first_output.laws_if_any:
* Relative Acceleration in Free Fall: \\(a_{\text{rel}} = a_A - a_B = (-g) - (-g) = 0\text{ [m/s}^2\text{]}\\)
* Relative Velocity in Free Fall: \\(v_{\text{rel}} = v_A - v_B = (v_{0A} - gt) - (v_{0B} - gt) = v_{0A} - v_{0B} = \text{constant [m/s]}\\)
* Interception Condition: \\(y_A(t_{\text{intercept}}) = y_B(t_{\text{intercept}})\text{ [m]}\\)
* Spatial Separation between Delayed Drops: \\(\Delta y(t) = v_{\text{rel}} \cdot t + \Delta y_0\text{ [m]}\\)
* Governing Limits: Valid as long as both bodies are simultaneously in unconstrained vertical free fall under identical gravity.
first_output.real_life_example:
